I step inside and put the register copy straight into Lord Edric's hands, then stay between him and Hale. "My lord, read this first. Your grandsire Aldous married Maud Fenn, a miller's daughter, in your own chapel, and Brother Osric will swear to it before Dame Crowe. The land is yours by plain deed, and the Aldermere line was Corvin's invention."

I turn to Hale with a bright smile. "And while you read, my lord, ask your steward why he wanted the book in my psalter, and why a man who 'merely attends' brought a hedge-carpenter named Garrow from Marrowford."

input.add_to_description: Day 2, ~6:30 PM: Wren's Persuasion (21) turned Lord Edric against him. Edric read the register copy, relieved at the plain deed, and ordered Hale confined to his room under guard pending the assessor's arrival; Garrow was held in the gatehouse. Hale made no scene and said only, "Corvin will not forgive this." Edric took back the spare key.

Day 2 evening: Lord Edric knows the truth, has confined Hale and Garrow, and will present the plain land-grant and Osric's attestation to Dame Crowe. Open threads: Corvin still upriver and will learn of this; Hale's warning; Wren's ledger remains hers.

entries.text:
You put the page into Lord Edric's hands and plant yourself between him and his steward. Your Persuasion check was a 21.

He reads it twice, his lips moving over *Maud Fenn, miller's daughter*. Then a long, shaky breath leaves him, and something eases in his face that you suspect hasn't eased in a month. "Plain deed," he whispers. "The land was always mine." He looks up at Hale, and the relief hardens into something colder. "A hedge-carpenter from Marrowford. The book in her psalter. Hale, I have trusted you with my purse for eleven years."

"My lord, the girl is a thief and a liar," Hale says gently. "She told you so herself."

"She told me, and she brought me a register. You have only ever told me what I wished to hear." Edric closes his hand on the key at his neck. "Two of the guards, Tobin. Master Hale will keep to his chamber until Dame Crowe arrives, and the carpenter to the gatehouse. Give me the spare key, Hale."

Hale surrenders it without a flicker. At the door, between two guards, he turns his head and meets your eyes, smiling at last. "Corvin will not forgive this, you know," he says softly. "He never forgives."

Then he is gone down the passage.

Lord Edric sinks into his chair and laughs, shakily, with tears on his face. "You came back to me. Whatever you owe Corvin, child, you owe me nothing, and I owe you a great deal." He promises supper, a bed in the manor, and a purse once Dame Crowe has gone. Tobin is grinning like a boy who has been let out of a cage.

It is a quarter to seven on Day 2. The assessor arrives at noon on Day 4. Corvin is upriver and will learn of this soon enough, and you still carry his ledger. For now you are safe, fed and welcome.

entries.text:
Your Persuasion check was a 13, and it lands.

You press the copy into Lord Edric's hands and step between him and his steward. He reads slowly, lips moving: *Aldous Verrel... Maud Fenn, miller's daughter.* His shoulders sag, but not with despair. It looks more like a long-held breath finally let go. "Maud Fenn," he whispers. "Grandmother. They told me she was a lady of Aldermere. I used to hate her portrait for how plain she looked."

Then he lifts his head and looks at Hale, and for the first time you see something of a lord in him. "A man who merely attends my accounts does not bring a hedge-carpenter from Marrowford, nor ask a chaplain for my family's register. Hale, the spare key. Now."

Hale studies him for a long moment. The smile holds. "As you wish, my lord." He unhooks a small iron key from his belt and sets it on the desk. He says nothing to you, but the look he gives you is as cold as river stone. Two of the gate guards, summoned by Tobin, walk him off to his quarters, where he'll stay until the assessor comes.

In the kitchen uproar, Garrow has slipped away. The back door stands open on the dusk.

Lord Edric sinks into his chair, holding the paper like something alive. "The land is mine by plain deed," he says. "I did not need any of it." He laughs, unsteadily. "Child, what do we tell Dame Crowe?"

Tobin hovers at your elbow, grinning with relief. It is half past six on Day 2. Dame Crowe arrives at noon on Day 4. You still hold Corvin's ledger, Corvin himself is somewhere upriver, and Garrow is loose in the night.

I do not yet believe the rest. Bring me proof of Hale's hand in this, something I can hold, and I'll dismiss him before Dame Crowe, but not on a kitchen's gossip."

Hale bows and withdraws, unhurried, Garrow trailing him. The door closes. You have until noon on Day 4 for proof. The ledger in your psalter may name Hale. Tonight you have a bed in the manor, and the household is awake and watching.

input.add_to_description: Day 3 evening: Marta Pell says Corvin's wagon stopped at midday, watered the horses, the driver bought bread and left in haste toward Ashby Weir. A brown-coated man asked if a half-elf lass with a lute had passed. Marta told him no, because she disliked his smile. Wren is given a bunk, supper and stabling for Biscuit.

entries.text:
The woman's face softens at the sight of the brass. "Marta Pell, keeper of the lamp. Come in, child, come in. Your mule can have the lean-to and a measure of oats, and you'll not pay a penny. That's the Bearer's rule."

Your Insight check was a 16, and it tells you she's honest and a little troubled. She says the shrine-wagon did stop, around midday. The driver watered his horses, bought a loaf, and left in a lather toward Ashby Weir without a word of blessing, which she thought unkind. A brown-coated man on a lathered horse came after, asking whether a half-elf lass with a lute had passed. "I said no. I didn't like his smile." She gives you a long, shrewd look. "Was I wrong to?"

Inside it is warm, with a hearth, a bunkroom of six plain cots (empty tonight), and a pot of leek-and-barley soup. The brass lamp burns on the mantel, and its light feels strangely like welcome. It is just past seven on Day 3.

Ashby Weir is another full day of road from here. The wagon has hours on you, and Garrow may be waiting somewhere ahead. Marta waits for your answer, ladle in hand.

input.description: Plump, grey-haired lay-keeper of Lantern's Rest. Honest and warm. Told Wren a shrine-wagon stopped at midday, the driver watered the horses, a man in a brown coat bought bread and a lame horse's liniment, and they pressed on toward Ashby Weir. Corvin was not aboard, but a hooded passenger sat inside and never got down; she thought she heard a coughing old voice.

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Marta Pell; added 1 relationship to Marta Pell

Marta Pell wipes her hands on her apron and goes quiet at the sight of the brass lantern. "Well, now. A true one." She touches two fingers to her brow in the road-god's sign. "In, love. Bed and bread are the Bearer's, not mine to sell, and your mule can have the lean-to and a bucket of oats."

While she bustles, you ask about the wagon. Your Insight check was a 16, and you can tell she holds nothing back. "Midday, aye. Painted with the same lamp as ours, which is why I looked twice. Driver watered the horses. A brown-coated fellow bought bread and liniment for a lame mare, rude as a wet cat. They never asked for beds. They pushed on toward Ashby Weir." She frowns. "Your master wasn't with them, if it's a master you're after. But there was someone inside the wagon who never got down, hooded, and I heard a cough, an old one. Not a man in a hurry, to my ear."

She sets you at the hearth with barley bread, hard cheese and a mug of hot cider. The bunkroom is empty, clean and warm. Outside the lamp burns steady on its pole, and the sky has gone fully dark. It's a little past seven.

Ashby Weir is another day's travel, and the wagon is half a day ahead. A hooded, coughing passenger who is not Corvin is a new piece of the puzzle.

input.description: Plump grey-haired widow, lay-keeper of Lantern's Rest. Honest and warm. Told Wren a shrine-wagon stopped at midday only to water the horses; the driver and a brown-coated man were in a hurry, asked the road to Ashby Weir, and left before one o'clock. The woman's face opens at the sight of the brass lantern. "Mother, is it? I'm Marta, and I'm no one's mother but my own two lads', but come in, love, come in." She takes Biscuit's rein herself and leads him to a lean-to stall with a bucket of oats.

Over the hearth, with barley broth and a heel of bread in front of you, she answers freely. Your Insight check was a 15, and you read nothing false in her. A shrine-wagon did stop, around midday, only long enough to water the horses. The driver was surly and a lean man in a brown coat was worse, short with her and quick with his eyes. They asked the road to Ashby Weir and were gone before one. Corvin wasn't with them, only those two. "And I didn't like him," she adds. "He smiled at my cat and the cat hid."

So the wagon is hours ahead, bound for Ashby Weir, with Garrow aboard and no Corvin yet. Wherever the storyteller is, he isn't on that wagon.

The bunkroom is clean, with a straw mattress and a blanket, and the keeper asks nothing but that you leave the lamp lit. It's just after seven. Ashby Weir is about a day's travel further, so you'd arrive tomorrow afternoon if you leave at dawn.

input.add_to_description: Marta Pell (Persuasion 11): Corvin gave the shrine its brass lamp seven years ago, saying it came "from an old friend, a road-priest who died on the Ashby road." The lamp's base is engraved with a looped inscription and a name worn almost smooth: "...ith Vael". Marta says Corvin wept when he hung it, which she thought odd for a man who "never prays." She does not know more.

Day 3 night: the lamp at Lantern's Rest was given by Corvin seven years ago from "an old friend, a road-priest who died on the Ashby road"; base engraved with worn name "...ith Vael" in looped script like the reliquary parchment. Possible link to Wren's origins.

entries.text:
Marta ladles you broth and settles across the hearth, glad of company. Your Persuasion check was an 11, enough to loosen her tongue.

"A road-priest? Now there's a thing." She wipes her hands. "Master Tallowmere gave us that lamp seven years back. Said it came from an old friend, a road-priest who died on the Ashby road, God keep her. He hung it himself, and I'll tell you, love, he wept doing it. A man who never prays, weeping at a lamp." She shakes her head. "I never asked."

She fetches a stool, and you take the lamp down together. The brass is warm and old. Round its base runs a line of looped, flowing script, worn nearly smooth by years of hands and weather. You can read only the tail of a name: *...ith Vael.* The loops are the same sweeping hand as the curl of parchment in your reliquary.

You pay for the bread with the story you promised, a tale of a lamp-bearer and a river, and Marta laughs and wipes her eyes in the right places. It's nearly eight. Corvin's note, the ledger and the lamp all point the same way: someone named Vael, a road-priest, dead on this road, and a man who wept.

The ford is two days off. The wagon is a day ahead. You've a bunk, a mule in a lean-to, and a long night.

entries.text:
You slip the note into the psalter beside the ledger pages and start on the broth. Your Persuasion check was a 16, and Marta warms like a banked fire.

"The lantern-case? Oh, he told me once, years back, over a cup too many," she says. "A road-priest gave it him, dying, on this very road. Brother Ansel Wick, a thin old fellow with a looped hand, always writing blessings for strangers. He asked that it go to 'a child who needs to be told the truth.'" She chuckles. "Master Tallowmere laughed when he said it, and never said a word more. I thought it was a joke."

She takes you out to the door and lifts the brass lamp down for you. On the base is a maker's mark: a tiny lantern with a looped letter W curling through it, the same loops as the parchment's script.

After supper you pay for the supper with a story, and she's delighted. Then she tucks you into a bunk with a wool blanket. The night is quiet, and Biscuit snores in the lean-to.

Brother Ansel Wick, then. A name, a road, and a purpose that someone had for you before you were ever a thief.

It's nearly eight on Day 3. Ashby Weir is a day's ride on, and Corvin expects you at the ford at dusk on Day 5. Do you rest here, and how do you want to approach tomorrow?

The broth is thick and good, and Marta settles across from you with her chin on her fist. Your Persuasion check was a 24, and it opens her up like a window.

"Old Wick," she says at once, as if the name had been waiting. "A real road-priest, the last I knew of, wrote in great loops like a child's drawing of waves. Corvin travelled with him years back, before my time here, and I only know it from Corvin's own telling. Wick died on this very road, and Corvin carried him here. They buried him under the lamp-pole." She nods toward the yard. "Corvin said Wick pressed a little brass lantern into his hands at the end and said, 'for the child.' He never said which child." You tuck the note into the psalter and take the broth. Your Persuasion check was a natural 20, and it opens Marta Pell like a window.

She talks until the bowls are empty. Corvin gave her the lamp over the door seven years ago, and she says he always paid his bed in stories. But the brass lantern-case, she says, he never claimed as his. "He told me once he was only the carrier. Said he'd promised an old friend."

It's in the book, nineteen years back, in looped, familiar letters, the same hand as the parchment in your reliquary. *A woman came through in the rain with a half-elf babe and gave no name. I wrote a blessing for the child of the lamp. I have put it in the brass case and given it to Master Tallowmere, who has sworn to carry it until she is grown. May he be better than his trade.*

Beneath it, in a different, later ink: *He did not say who she was. I did not ask.*

The lamp over the door, when you see it, is a plain brass lantern with a worn base, nothing hidden. But the case in your pack was never stolen. It was yours, carried by the man you ran from.

Marta watches you gently and asks for her story. It's nearly eight, there's a bunk waiting, and the ford at Ashby Weir lies a day's ride away, with Corvin there on the fifth day.

What does Wren do?

You fold the note into the psalter and sit to the broth. Your Persuasion check was a 15, and Marta needs little coaxing once the bowl is empty and you've promised a story.

"Anselm," she says, and her face softens. "Old Brother Anselm. Eighteen years back, it was, before my Tam died. A road-priest, thin as a heron, wrote blessings in great looping letters and gave them away to anyone who'd stand still. He took a fever on the road and we laid him in the back bunk there. There was a young player with him, a skinny lad with a gift for voices, who'd been walking with him a season. Corvin." She sniffs. "Sat up four nights with him. Wept at the burying like a child. Then he took the old man's brass lantern-case and went on his way, and the next I saw him he was fine and prosperous and quite a different sort of man."

She lifts you up to the door, and you take the brass lamp down from its pole. The rays on the shutters match your reliquary. Under the base, scratched small and worn, are the words *For A., who lit it. C.*

The lamp over the door was Anselm's. The case in your pack was his too. Corvin gave one to the shrine, kept the other, and let you keep it.

You tell Marta the story you promised, a quiet one about a lantern that walked a road by itself, and she cries a little and laughs at the end. By eight the common room is warm and dim, the mule is fed, and the bunk is clean. The ford at Ashby Weir is a day and a half ahead, Corvin's wagon a few hours.

Your Persuasion check was a 17. Marta pulls her stool close to the hearth, and the story pours out of her the way stories do when someone listens.

"Seven years back, it was. He came through in a storm with a half-grown girl wrapped in his cloak, burning with fever. You, love, I'd stake my apron on it. He sat up three nights in that bunkroom wiping your brow and never once told a story, and I'd never known him not to. When you mended, he paid for the lamp over the door and was gone before the thanks."

She doesn't know who gave Corvin the brass case. But the looped hand rings a bell. "Our founder wrote like that. Sister Ysolde Marrin, a road-priest, who built this place with her own hands and then walked off down the road one spring and never came back. Corvin asked me about her once, years ago, then went quiet as a stone."

She takes the lamp from its pole and lets you turn it in the firelight. On the underside of the base, small and worn, is a line in looping script: *Lit for the one who comes after.*

You've the same loops in your own reliquary, and a note from Corvin telling you to ask who wrote them. It's past eight now, the broth is cold, and the bunk is waiting. The wagon is a day ahead, the ford is two days off, and you still owe Marta a story.

What does Wren do?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.
